title: Scoops in three cups
hook: Dividing always makes a number smaller. Or does it?

knows: fractions as equal parts of a whole (a quarter is one of four equal parts)
division as sharing or as 'how many fit'
doesNotKnow: why dividing by a fraction gives a bigger number
that dividing by 1/n is the same as multiplying by n

misconception: Dividing always makes a number smaller.
objective: The learner can explain 3 / (1/4) = 12 as 'four quarter-cup scoops per cup, three cups', and say that dividing by 1/n multiplies by n.

claims.text: Twelve 1/4-cup scoops fit in 3 cups: 3 / (1/4) = 3 x 4 = 12.
claims.source: Four quarters make one cup, so 3 cups hold 3 x 4 = 12 quarter-cup scoops; the stage draws 3 columns of 4 numbered scoops; recomputed with node.

claims.text: With a 1/n-cup scoop, each cup holds n scoops, so 3 cups hold 3 x n (1 cup: 3, 1/2: 6, 1/3: 9, 1/4: 12, 1/5: 15).
claims.source: n pieces of size 1/n make 1; recomputed with node for n = 1..5.

claims.text: Dividing by 1/n is the same as multiplying by n, so dividing by a number smaller than 1 gives a bigger answer.
claims.source: a / (1/n) is the number x with x * (1/n) = a, so x = a * n; for 0 < d < 1, a / d > a when a > 0.

claims.text: Division can be read as 'how many of these fit?' (measurement or quotitive division).
claims.source: The quotitive (measurement) model of division, e.g. National Research Council, Adding It Up (2001), ch. 3 and ch. 7 on fraction division.

recall.question: A ribbon is 2 metres long. How many pieces of 1/3 metre can you cut from it?
recall.why: Each metre holds three 1/3-metre pieces, so 2 / (1/3) = 2 x 3 = 6. Dividing by a fraction asks how many fit.
